name: Priya Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 58, and a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I changed work after the cinema where I'd worked closed, and I'm still slower and less skilled than the experienced crew. Today I prepared cable routes and helped fit parts under supervision, with the senior worker correcting how I'd read a drawing. I like understanding a room by the end of a job, but asking someone younger to explain a mark again can make me feel foolish.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a laundry, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent our home. I earn typical pay for the trade, we've saved four months of normal expenses and there are some similar electrical employers nearby. I use AI occasionally for a study explanation after a colleague has shown the tool works, then check practical questions with the supervisor. I think people should get paid teaching rather than finance every change alone. Retirement is something I want to understand, but I haven't verified what our old work records would provide or when, if anything.

say: I'd welcome **less noise** and keep useful study explanations without replacing the senior worker teaching me.
I'd still ask why **the drawing** matches the actual room before moving on with the practical task.
think: Our **wages and reserve** cover ordinary living, with four months saved against interruptions.
Being a **slow beginner** can hurt my pride without making the household rent uncertain in this mild picture.
do: Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting work now and through the first plateau year.
Keep the **familiar budget** and occasional checked study explanations, requesting practical checks rather than buying another course.
feel: **Calm** about household money, with ordinary frustration at needing repeated explanation.
S0.quote: A clear paragraph isn't the same as a hand that knows where to mark.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on typical pay, covering wages and a moderate reserve; junior mistakes cause embarrassment without current income alarm.
She retains **practical supervision**, treating occasional AI explanations as existing study and held cash as a reserve rather than retirement income.

steps.text: Continue supervised preparation and fitting with practical checks and the familiar household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little less noise would give us space to do a decent day's work. I'd keep a useful study explanation without asking it to replace a senior worker. I'd still want to know why a drawing matched the room in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the ordinary bills, and four months saved gives us a reasonable reserve. I'd feel secure about our living over the next few years if the practical work continued much as it does now. Being slow at a new job can bruise my pride without making the rent uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep doing the supervised preparation and fitting work. Through the first plateau year I'd keep the familiar budget and occasional checked study explanations, rather than buy another course to look busy. I'd ask for the same practical checks I already need before going on to an unfamiliar task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, with ordinary frustration when I need something explained twice. I'd be relieved to keep learning without another urgent demand to start over. I could enjoy a walk with my partner after work instead of treating every evening as preparation time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the study explanation sounded clear but the drawing still confused you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hadn't understood it and ask the senior worker. A clear paragraph isn't the same as a hand that knows where to mark. I don't want embarrassment to decide which checks I ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the quiet picture change how you used the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave it available for actual household trouble rather than spend it because the future sounded quieter. That's money we've already saved, not a new saving action. I still wouldn't call the reserve a retirement income.

say: I'd ask **faster planning** to retain practical teaching for the beginner who still fits the part.
I'd include **older learners** in a shared request for paid practice and clear instructions.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink if the firm squeezed the time given to slower beginners.
Our **four-month reserve** gives response time, without removing worry about losing income before becoming properly useful.
do: Join the **workers' association** and request named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained.
Keep **supervised work**, recording actual paid hours monthly and relying on no practice arrangement before written agreement.
feel: **Anxious** about income and practical progress, while still willing to learn through checked demonstrations.
S1.quote: A signature from the crew isn't the employer's agreement.
fieldNote: She identifies **own-hour risk** despite a moderate reserve, rather than substituting general discomfort about software for a household income concern.
Her **collective action** is membership and a signed request; the proposed paid practice isn't counted as agreed or delivered.

steps.text: Join the association and request named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained
Keep supervised work; record paid hours monthly and rely on no arrangement before written agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning should leave time to teach the person fitting the part. I'd sign a shared request through the workers' association for paid practice and clear instructions. I wouldn't want people my age quietly left out because somebody assumed we were leaving soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if the firm squeezed the time it allowed slower beginners, even while practical work remained. Four months saved would help us respond, but I'd still worry about losing a wage while trying to get properly useful. I'd have to check actual paid hours rather than assume the job title was protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the workers' association and sign a request for named supervised practice during paid hours with normal wages retained. In the first year I'd keep the current supervised work and record actual paid hours monthly. I'd rely on no proposed practice arrangement until the employer agreed it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about income and progress, but still willing to learn something that had proved useful. I'd want time to repeat a practical task. I'd hate to be handed a link and told that counted as paid teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice request need to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for an experienced person to demonstrate, watch me repeat and check the result inside the paid day. I wouldn't claim the arrangement existed because we'd signed a request. A signature from the crew isn't the employer's agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm required an unfamiliar electronic form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what paid instruction and checks came with it before being expected to send a record. I wouldn't pretend I knew the system to keep a meeting short. Knowing I need a demonstration is part of being honest about the work.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** at age 60 from robots around 2031 at age 63.
I'd check **paid work and resources** rather than assume approaching retirement protects either date.
think: Both **physical household jobs** could lose hours as capable robots spread, without a known purchase timetable or certain total loss.
I'd still need **verified retirement information** before treating any future income as a replacement for wages.
do: Request **association advice** on official records and support eligibility, checking availability and assuming no payment.
Save **50 extra monthly** from new wages after essentials only while both incomes hold, stopping if either income falls or surplus disappears.
Keep **suitable supervised work** during 2029 only while available, comparing actual income and essential costs monthly.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with a reserve, advice requests and small conditional deposits providing some control.
S2.quote: A request for information isn't a pension payment.
fieldNote: Her **anxiety** follows possible wage loss without a known machine price or certain total loss, leaving room for action.
The **new saving** uses wage surplus, stops if either income falls or surplus disappears, and never relabels existing emergency cash.

steps.text: Request association help obtaining official retirement information and checking eligibility, assuming no availability or payment
Save 50 monthly from new wage surplus after essentials only while both paid incomes hold
Stop extra saving if either income falls or surplus disappears, leaving existing reserves untouched
Keep suitable supervised paid work during 2029 only while available; review actual household figures monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 when I'd be 60, with capable robots around 2031 when I'd be 63. I'd use the gap to check paid work and real household resources. I wouldn't assume being near retirement made either date harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink as firms prepared for capable hands-on machines, and my partner's laundry work could face the later change too. I don't know machine prices or what employers would buy first, so I can't predict a total wage loss. I would be anxious about needing income before we had checked the retirement records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the association's advice service whether it could help us obtain official retirement information and check support eligibility, without assuming availability or any payment. We'd save fifty extra monthly only from new wages after essentials while both paid incomes held, stopping if either fell or surplus disappeared. During 2029 I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and compare actual income and essential costs monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some control through the reserve and the people we could ask. I'd feel less secure about future wages than in the plateau, but not certain the whole wage was already gone. I'd want figures rather than a reassuring age label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the advice service to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring actual wage records, essential bills and the old employment papers we could find. I'd ask what official record was missing and when any confirmed income could be available. A request for information isn't a pension payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you could not keep up the extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop it before borrowing or moving money from the existing four months. It would be a small new wage deposit, not a target we had to protect at the expense of bills. I'd want my partner to see the real amount, including a month when it was zero.

say: I'd use **five years** to seek proper paid learning now rather than leave older beginners waiting.
I'd keep **ages 63 and 66** visible without treating either age as an entitlement to a funded exit.
think: More time could improve my practical work, but **paid hours** could still shrink during the change.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace verified retirement figures or fund a permanent exit by itself.
do: Maintain the **shared paid-practice request** and request record advice, subject to actual availability.
Save **50 extra monthly** only from new wages after essentials while both incomes hold, stopping after either falls or surplus disappears.
Compare **verified income and essentials** during 2032 before any exit decision, using confirmed wages while records remain unresolved.
feel: **Anxious** about income and resources, with more time for practical learning and accurate records.
S3.quote: Learning slowly doesn't mean every new certificate is the answer.
fieldNote: She retains **own-income risk** and an unresolved retirement budget, while explaining what extra time changes about practical learning and checking records.
Her **course enquiry** remains unchosen; incomplete records prompt further checking rather than invented income, dates or automatic rejection of possible resources.

steps.text: Maintain the shared request for named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained
Request association record advice subject to availability, counting no unverified retirement income or support
Save 50 monthly from new wage surplus after essentials while both incomes hold; stop without surplus
Delay work-exit decisions until verified income and essential costs have been compared during 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should give an older beginner proper paid learning time, not just a longer period of waiting. I'd be 63 when thinking work changed in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still ask through the association now, while I was doing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could improve at practical tasks in the extra years, but my paid hours could still shrink during the change. I'd be anxious about relying on wages without confirmed retirement figures at 63 or 66. Four months saved is useful time to check, not a funded exit by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd maintain the shared request for named paid practice and ask the advice service about record help, subject to availability. We'd keep the fifty extra monthly deposit only from new wages after essentials while both paid incomes held, stopping if either fell or surplus disappeared. During 2032 we'd compare verified income and essential costs before deciding whether I could leave suitable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the resource question, but more able to learn before the later machines. I'd hope to make a better decision with the actual records in front of us. I wouldn't let another three years stand in for a confirmed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the official records were incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the provider or former employer how to correct it and keep the budget on confirmed wages meanwhile. I'd ask for help with the paperwork rather than guess the amount or starting date. I wouldn't treat a missing record as either guaranteed money or proof there was none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in a new course just because there was more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't chosen or funded another course. I'd ask for named paid teaching on the actual tasks and check any real course terms if one was offered. Learning slowly doesn't mean every new certificate is the answer.

say: I'd use **ten years** to check later work and resources rather than assume older people are automatically protected.
I'd retain **paid teaching now** while keeping ages 68 and 71 explicit in the longer household discussion.
think: Present wages and our **four-month reserve** make near-term living secure while the later income question remains unresolved.
I cannot assume **income or work capacity** at 68, or count grown children's possible wages as household resources.
do: Keep **suitable supervised work** now while available and maintain the shared paid-practice request.
Request **association record help**, subject to availability, counting no unverified pension, support or family payment.
Compare **confirmed income and essentials** during 2037 with actual capacity and suitable work options before deciding on an exit.
feel: **Uneasy** about later resources, while near-term security leaves room for ordinary life and careful checking.
S4.quote: I wouldn't call the distant date a guarantee of health or a job.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **near-term security** from actual retirement resources and later work capacity, counting no future entitlement or job merely from her age.
Her **children's help** requires agreement, while changed wages, costs or health bring resource checking forward rather than waiting for the date.

steps.text: Keep suitable supervised paid work now only while available
Maintain the shared request for named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained
Request association record help subject to availability, counting no unverified pension, support or family contribution
Compare confirmed income, essentials, actual capacity and suitable work during 2037 before any exit decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to check what later work and retirement actually mean, rather than assume every older person is protected. I'd be 68 when thinking work changed in 2036 and about 71 when robots followed around 2039. I'd still want paid teaching while I needed the current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present wages and four-month reserve make the next few years look secure in this slower picture, though the later income question is on my mind. I can't assume retirement income or a suitable physical job at 68. The grown children have their own lives, and their possible wages aren't ours to put in a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and the shared request for paid practice active. I'd request help checking official records through the association service, subject to availability, counting no unverified pension, support or family payment. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed income, essential costs and my actual ability and suitable work options before choosing any exit or further work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later years, but able to enjoy our ordinary life now. I'd feel better having time to ask for the actual figures rather than choose from a birthday. I wouldn't call the distant date a guarantee of health or a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count from the grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through help they had actually chosen and we had agreed. I'd first ask for help understanding the records, not assign either child a rent payment. I'd want their own needs in the conversation too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you check sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real wage change, essential cost or health change would bring the review forward. I'd use the actual figures rather than wait for 2036. I'd also ask for missing records now instead of making the long warning an excuse to leave the papers unopened.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior hours could shrink while we still needed the wage and hadn't checked the next income. Named paid practical teaching, normal wages protected and accessible advice on the official records would help. Four months saved gives me time to ask properly, not an answer about when I can stop earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a person has a reserve and still needs someone to explain the retirement papers. I can learn a new task and still not know which old employer has the record. I'd rather ask twice than turn a guess into a household budget.

headlineQuote: Four months saved gives me time to ask properly, not an answer about when I can stop earning.
portrait: **Priya, 58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and a need for supervision.
Her **household** has a partner, grown children, rented housing, typical trade pay, four months saved and some nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI occasionally after proof**, favours shared paid teaching and checks official retirement records without assuming an income or appointment.
Possible **hours losses** create anxiety in faster worlds; longer warnings don't guarantee retirement resources, physical capacity or a job at 68.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink junior hours before the household checks what dependable income comes next.
whatWouldHelp: Named **paid practical teaching** with normal wages protected would make learning achievable.
Accessible advice on **official retirement records** would clarify real resources without assuming entitlement, payment or appointment.
